Historically, parties here have been formed around a man.
Lemus, by abdicating in favor of Rubio Melhado as party manager, sacrificed his place as leader and it is doubtful that PRUD as it is now constituted will be vary decisive factor in current crisis. 5.
Osorio Clique. Ex-President Osorio still represents strongest non-Communist political force in country. He has loyal adherents in all strata and his reservoir of strength runs deep. Close friends quote him as desirous of seeing Lemus complete term despite deep differences but there is evidence that his lieutenants have been exceedingly active since the present crisis began. We doubt Osorio will step forward until called but believe his ear is cocked to catch weakest summons.
Osorio as a man is better known to several now in ARA than to us here. Our impression, however, is that Osorio would have liked to have been more reformist than he was during his term. He held back mainly by more conservative wealthy elements on whose monetary support he heavily depended. We do not believe the same situation will exist again and that Osario would be inclined to be rather liberal in his outlook and policies. This view reinforced by type people considered close associates such as Jorge SOL Castellanos. We would not expect Osorio to be openly antagonistic to U.S., or West. Neither would we expect him to be as openly pro-U.S. or as amenable to suggestions from us as has been Lemus government. While not favorable to Castroism we believe he would attempt to apply some Castro-type reform measures here. 6.
Labor. Communist-dominated CUTS with 3,000 members is one prime movers current anti-government drive. Non-[illegible in the original]CGS with 20,000 controls large majority organized labor. CGS is considered relatively free from Castro influences. To date it has rejected the oppositionists’ appeal for general strike and we believe it will continue to do so. CGS leadership not close to Lemus, however, and complains of inability to [illegible in the original] him to discuss programs. Perhaps significant that CGS has not during present crisis publicly proclaimed support of government. Moreover current government efforts unseat Secretary-General Saravia will probably result in CGS schism, leaving majority under Saravia even less disposed work in Lemus’ behalf. Despite this conflict, CGS leadership, including Saravia, privately proclaim support for constitutional government. Saravia known to be in close touch with Osorio group, however, and should situation deteriorate further, possibility open swing to Osorio should not be discounted.
7.
Congress. Handpicked and representing hard-core what remains PRUD party, Congress can be expected to do Lemus’ bidding. Method of election and mediocrity of membership have, however, left it without much respect throughout country. Its deliberations for most part go unheralded and its power as a political force considered minimal. Assembly President Esquivel is friend both Lemus and Osorio; private conversations lead me to believe he has preference for latter. 8.
University. This institution has long been one of principal targets of Communist infiltration and results achieved true cause for alarm. All major student organizations are in hands Communist or pro-Communist elements and faculty itself includes several extreme leftist types. Success in part, due practice keeping professional agitators and organizers matriculated as students for up to ten years. While this element represents small minority total student body, its influence greatly disproportionate to size. We are reliably informed that control over students who had no desire take part current political activities gained largely through intimidation and coercion. Only small minority student body took part in disturbances at outset current crisis, with large majority strongly opposed to involvement. Police action and clever handling by student agitators were effective in turning majority against Lemus and our information indicates that majority still considers him public enemy number one. Past week has provided a cooling off period, however, and signs beginning to appear that student body in general tiring of being used and started to think of personal loss ensuing from closed University. Number private groups also forming with aim providing anti-Castro/Communist students with rallying points and with physical protection against coercive efforts if needed. Students here as elsewhere have no positive program—they are only against the existing order and in their search for a cause or philosophy they are prey to
highly obtained purposeful and, unfortunately, extremely versatile and able student leaders in international communism’s pay. As a group, they still do not appear to have been completely disabused of their illusions with respect to Castroism and what it stands for. One thing is clear: Lemus is anathema to the large majority and is unlikely ever to re-win students’ confidence or support. 9.
Campesino. Thus far this overwhelming majority had taken no part in current disturbances. The campesino has [illegible in the original] some interest as a spectator but no propensity to include his voice of his “machete” in current happenings. Embassy knows that travelling pro-Castro/Communist teams have been proselytizing to the countryside but as yet they do not appear to have succeeded in setting
imaginations afire. Lemus, as a President, is thought to be relatively popular among this class, but as a man, Osorio is still reversed by the campesino and the “little” man of Salvador. Thus, while dormant at the moment, the campesino is not happy or content with his lot and a spark in the right place could set this very volatile element afire. Moreover, should the situation in the capital become chaotic at any time, the campesino’s weight can be expected to make itself felt.

While the fall of the Lemus government does not appear imminent, should it occur, it would in all likelihood take the form of a voluntary abdication or ouster. In case of the former, the Vice President constitutionally would succeed to office, i.e., in the following order: Costa, Esquivel, Alvarez, Escapini. None is a military man. While much would depend on attendant circumstances, there is a strong chance that the military would intervene and set up a governing Junta with the results described below.

If Lemus were ousted, the Communists would not be in a position to seize control. The Osorio strategy and tactics to [illegible in the original] have been effectively hidden and would seem to indicate that he would continue to remain in the background and refrain from immediately taking over. However, the possibility should not be entirely discounted.

The most likely development in case of an ouster would be a military Junta. In such case the odds are that the power would shortly thereafter be transferred to Osorio, who would seek to constitutionalize his tenure, possibly through elections.

The advent of Osorio would still keep El Salvador oriented toward the West and favorable towards the Osorio but by no means as friendly as under the present government. I am not completely certain that Osorio would return to his former strong anti-Communist position although there is good reason to believe that in deference to the military he would do so. The winds of nationalism are blowing more strongly here than for some time. Criticism of the U.S. has been stirred from
Cuba and has been increasingly evident in student and labor publications and meetings. Castroism has its adherents. Osorio coming to power against this background could not help but be responsive in some measure to its pressures, some of which would be bound to react unfavorably against the United States.

Therefore, as long as the present situation does not deteriorate, we continue to hope that constitutional government can be preserved here and believe that Lemus still has it within his power to save it.

To that end I recommend that we provide Lemus with short-term aid by immediate implementation on a crash basis of the program set forth in Embassy despatches 21 of July 26, 1960See Document ES–17. and 62 of September 7, 1960,Under conver of despatch 62, Ambassador Kalijarvi transmitted an ICA survey team report of August 24, which recommended the addition of an investigation advisor to the two-man staff of the ICA Public Safety Program in El Salvador. (716.5-MSP/9–760) A Public Safety Advisor, John C. Hazelett, was added to the ICA Public Safety Program staff on December 31, 1961. [text not declassified] and also by immediate implementation of the program discussed in correspondence between Mr. Charles E. Higdon of ARA and the Embassy including the letter of Mr. Downs to Mr. Higdon dated August 26, 1960. We should also press forward with long-term economic and social assistance and with the Central American Bank. Lemus needs to make new advances with economic and social programs, if he survives. If he does not survive, we need to consolidate our position with a successor government through such programs as are not designed to support any particular administration but to improve the country as a whole. In either case the United States should provide assistance of a longer-term nature in the economic and social fields. We shall submit separate recommendations accordingly.

div.head: ES–24. Airgram From the Embassy in El Salvador to the Department of StateSource: Department of State, Central Files. 4 pages not declassified.
ES–25. Editorial Note
div.p: At 6:00 a.m. on October 26, 1960, a group of Salvadorans, civilian and military, claiming the constitutional right of insurrection and acting with the support of the armed forces, deposed the Government of President Lemus. A Junta, consisting of three military and three civilian members, assumed legislative and executive powers. In a bulletin issued on October 26, the Junta announced that the Constitution and laws remained in effect; guaranteed the rights of citizens; and promised to hold free elections. (Telegram 220 from San Salvador, October 27, 1960; 716.00/10–2760)

Newly appointed Salvadoran Foreign Minister Rolando Déneke wrote to Ambassador Kalijarvi on October 27, referring to the over-throw of the Lemus government and stating that the Junta wished to maintain very close and cordial relations with the United States Government. (Note quoted in telegram 222 from San Salvador, October 27, 1960; 716.00/10–2760)

div.head: ES–26. Telegram from the Ambassador in El Salvador (Kalijarvi) to the Department of StateSource: Department of State, Central Files, 716.00/10–2960. Secret; Priority.
div.p: 233. Analyzing composition new junta and government it is difficult escape conclusion that there has been a decided shift to the left in complexion government of El Salvador.

While most of those appointed to key posts on military side thought basically friendly to the U.S. and democratically inclined, they are, with two or three exceptions, young, of middle grade and wholly inexperienced both in affairs of government and political intrigue. Civilian side of government provides grounds for real concern. High percentage of them have, at the least, questionable backgrounds. Four civilian cabinet officers believed out and out Commies; four are very leftist and at least two more known to be exceedingly liberal and revolutionary minded. Even more ominous, however, are appointments to
second and third echelon posts now emerging, e.g., Salazar Rodezno as Public Information Officer of Casa Presidencial. Disturbing number those recently exiled and who were in forefront in leading cheers for Castro now being given second echelon posts.

Turning to coup itself, evidence rapidly accumulating that it masterminded by and executed under direction of ex-president Osorio. Substantial evidence also indicates that nerve center in Ministry of Defense, with Generals Parada and especially Lopez Ayala utilizing Guardia Nacional rather than army to carry out overthrow. Also good reason to believe that Osorio, in planning coup, effected marriage of convenience with extreme leftist and other dissident oppositionist forces, including General Quintanilla and Captain Buitrago, who
confirmed as actual Lemus abductors. There can be no arguing that coup masterpiece of planning and execution. No bloodshed, no disruption of public services. Although impressive number high ranking army officers given short period opt for or against junta and number those refusing subsequently relieved, no resistance any nature offered. Considerable evidence however that large sums of money changed hands, some of which reportedly of Cuban origin.

In putting together this military-civilian coalition, Osorio doubtless reasoned that he could control it. He probably also reasoned that cooperation with left was necessary both in planning stages and now for overthrow to be successful at this time. Inclusion this civilian element probably intended as sop to students and PRAM elements in effort gain their cooperation in stabilizing situation and gaining as wide acceptance of overthrow as possible until he prepared for next move. It may be that he intends move in on pro-Commie elements then in RakosiMátyás Rákosi, former Hungarian Communist leader.-like salami tactic. Present indications, however, are that plan is to allow junta to govern until regular election time in 1962 when Osorio will emerge as favorite son candidate.

It seems to us that many dangers are inherent in this reasoning and that situation as it stands today leaves many extremely important questions unanswered: 1.
Osorio has not yet shown his hand and while it is generally assumed that he is man behind throne, is he in fact? Neither the public nor we have any real proof. 2.
If he is in fact the strong man, how deep does his control extend, especially into the civilian side? Will he be able to control the Commies in his government? 3.
What commitments did he make in order to gain left-wing cooperation? 4.
What are his real intentions with respect to life span of junta and free elections?
5.
Where did the money used in the coup come from?

We are convinced from pattern of coup, make-up and early actions of government, Communist tones of decrees and announcements, and especially yesterday’s press conference by junta (EMBTEL 231)Telegram 231, October 29, 1960 reported that the civilian members of the Junta dominated the press conference. (716.00/10–2960) that military element no match for civilian leftists and that as matters now stand, we must regard coup as first step towards Fidelismo. For moment announcements seem calculated to lull us but clearly next stage will be struggle for power between Commies and more conservative element and military with odds favoring former.

If remedial measures to be successful they will have to be taken within next few days while army still has control of arms. Reports reaching us indicate that while many viewed coup with approval at outset believing Osorio was the man, their ardor has cooled considerably after seeing make-up of government. A counter coup effort, therefore, which our information indicates may be in making, may find more public support outside leftist elements than could have been hoped for earlier.

View all these considerations and many still unanswered questions, believe strongly that our traditional policy of recognition should not be following in this instance. If our fears confirmed by subsequent action, major and practically only weapon available to U.S., since intervention renounced under international agreement, is recognition and/or nonrecognition. Believe from talks with colleagues our action in this respect will be closely watched and followed by number of other countries. I urge with all persuasiveness at my command the Department go slow with recognition.

div.head: ES–27. Memorandum from the Assistant Secretary of State for Inter-American Affairs (Mann) to the Secretary of StateSource: Department of State, S/S NSC (Miscellaneous) Files, Lot 66 D 95, “NSC–5902 Memoranda.” Secret. Drafted by Gwynn and Higdon, and initialed for Mann by Gwynn.

list.head: SUBJECT
list.item: Coup d’etat in El Salvador

div.p: In the early hours of October 26 a bloodless coup d’etat occurred in El Salvador which resulted in the sending of strongly pro-U.S. president Jose Maria Lemus and his principal aide and heir apparent, Major Adolfo Rubio Melhado into forced exile in San Jose, Costa Rica, and the assumption of power by the following six-man combined military civilian Junta.
Military Members:

Col. César Yanes Urías—Deputy Chief of General Staff under Lemus regime. Recently assigned to special staff responsible for maintaining order in San Salvador during state of siege. Has been in the U.S.; described by former U.S. Military Attaché to El Salvador (Col. Ferguson) as reticent, non-commital, retiring in personality; not particularly a leader.

Lt. Col. Miguel Angel Castillo— Director of the Treasury Police under Lemus regime; former Director General of Telecommunications under President Osorio; described by former USMA as friend of President Osorio, a leader, and very friendly to U.S. (The Auxiliary Bishop of Guatemala, who spent many years in El Salvador, describes both Yanes and Castillo as “high-calibre anti-Communist officers of the Osorio stripe.”)

Major Ruben Alonso Rosales—former Deputy Chief of key El Zapote Fortress, commanding the capital city of San Salvador; described by former USMA as being very friendly to a former member of U.S. Army mission; close to General Parada, late Minister of Defense, known as friendly to U.S.
Civilian Members:

Dr. Fabio Castillo—Medical Doctor and Vice Dean of the School of Medicine at the National University; respected and popular with University students; has studied in the U.S. and Europe; a known liberal or leftist, who has been called “Communist”, a charge which has not been substantiated.

Rene Fortin Magana—Lawyer, aged 30. As a University student was an active leftist, anti-U.S., an associate of Communists, and an alleged “Communist.” A Salvadoran source here, however, whose judgment I value, described him as young, honorable, violent, rich, and not left. In view of my personal knowledge of the University of El Salvador, I am inclined to the latter view.

Ricardo Falla Caceres—Lawyer, aged 32. An active leftist at the University in recent years who has been consistently alleged to be a “Communist,” but is described as liberal by other sources considered reliable.

The individuals comprising the Junta and the new cabinet appear to represent a cross-section of Salvadoran political views. This is undoubtedly deliberate, in an endeavor to attract widespread support for the new Government. They are largely younger men who are relatively unknown politically. A tentative appraisal indicates that the new Government is nearer the “middle of the road” than to either extreme, with a definite tendency towards the left on the part of the civilian members. Ambassador Kalijarvi views a substantial proportion of the civilian members as being to the extreme left. The Department’s sources indicate many of them to be moderates, although preponderantly to the left.

The new Government’s first actions have been to release political prisoners, lift the state of siege, cancel the law restricting the right of assembly, and to announce that it would hold free elections as scheduled in 1962 and would govern by means of decrees during the transitory period of government. Also, it has declared its firm intention to comply strictly with the political Constitution of 1950, to respect existing treaties and international conventions, to fulfill its obligations and commitments, and to respect human rights. These latter assurances have been given by the new Minister of Foreign Affairs in a note dated October 27 to our Embassy in San Salvador.The text of the Note was translated in telegram 222 from San Salvador, October 27, 1960. (716.00/10–2760)

Among the principal factors leading to the overthrow of the Lemus Government have been (a) his failure to carry out social reforms announced following his inauguration in 1956; (b) his failure to accept the advice of and delegate responsibility to the better-qualified members of his cabinet; (c) his vacillation in controlling the increasing activities of pro-Castro and pro-Communist agitators, first by failure to act and later through strong-arm suppression; and (d) his alienation of the military by his apparent intention to make his aide, Major Rubio Melhado, his successor to the Presidency.

The coup d’etat followed over two months of demonstrations by anti-Government and student and labor groups, initiated on August 16 by a protest against the existing regime and the OAS Meeting of Foreign Ministers at San Jose. President Lemus was finally goaded, principally by the Salvadoran press, into using repressive measures against the demonstrators, including the arrest and exile of agitators, the enacting of a law restricting the right of assembly, excessive force by members of the security units, and the establishment of a state of siege, which soon alienated most of Lemus’ own supporters and created martyrs for continued anti-Government agitation. Temporary truces were effected by a civilian group composed of representatives of the Church, prominent businessmen, and representatives of the leading families, which intervened in an effort to mediate the differences between the Lemus Government and the demonstrators. These efforts, and less violent measures by the Security Forces, produced over a month of relative calm immediately preceding the unexpected coup d’etat, which appears to have been carried out as a preventative measure to insure that pro-Castro and pro-Communist elements would be unable to capitalize on the constantly deteriorating stability of the Lemus regime.

The files of U.S. intelligence agencies contain reports indicating that the three civilian members of the Junta and a number of the members of the new cabinet have been accused of being “Communists,” pro-Communist, and/or associates of Communists. Such accusations have been levelled at one time or another against almost all “liberals” or “leftists” in El Salvador who have advocated change in their still largely semi-feudal social order, opponents of the regime in power, and/or students politically active in the affairs of the traditionally leftist-oriented, anti-status quo, and anti-Government University. The term “Communist” is frequently used synonymously with “leftist” in El Salvador. As a result some of the best friends of the U.S., and some of the most effective anti-Communist leaders in El Salvador (including former President Osorio and several of his trusted associates), have been bitterly denounced as “Communists”. Therefore, ARA believes it would be a grave error to consider, without further substantiating evidence, that the new Government or its members are suspect for this reason, in the absence of their identification with purely Communist objectives.

From information now being received from a variety of sources it appears that able Ex-President Oscar Osorio is emerging as the dominant personality behind the Coup. However, the political orientation and likely policies of the new government, while controversial, indicate a definite swing to the left in El Salvador. On the other hand, ARA
[Remaining is missing in source text]

div.head: ES–28. Memorandum for the President by the Secretary of State.Source: Department of State, Central Files, 716.02/11–260. Secret. Drafted by William T. Pryce, Staff Aide, Bureau of Inter-American Affairs. It was transmitted to Secretary Herter by covering memorandum from Assistant Secretary Mann, November 1, 1960. In his memorandum, Mann elaborated the points made above in favor of recognition and recommended that the Secretary sign the present memorandum to the President. (716.02/11–160)

list.head: SUBJECT
list.item: Recognition of the New Regime in El Salvador

div.p: The six-man Junta which assumed power in El Salvador on October 26 is pressing for recognition by the United States.

There is some evidence that this is a government somewhat to the left of that of former President Lemus and that a majority of the members of the Junta and Cabinet are anti-Communist, although a small minority are not particularly desirable from our point of view. Moreover, there is a report that a counter-coup may be attempted.

Nevertheless, the weight of evidence is that the majority of the Army and the conservative oligarchy support the present government. It is generally believed that the most prominent, if not the dominant, figure in this movement is former President Oscar Osorio, President Lemus’ predecessor, who has a long record of cooperation with the United States and of opposition to communist domination of El Salvador’s political life. The Embassy of El Salvador in Washington has issued a press release saying in part that the “Members of the Civic-Military Junta had emphatically declared in a press conference that the revolutionary movement they represent is strictly national and authentically democratic, consistent with the basic principles of Western democracy without any ties, whatsoever, with foreign powers or ideologies.”

The Governments of Guatemala, Honduras, Panama, Ecuador, Uruguay, Argentina, Spain and Mexico have already recognized, and it is probable that other recognitions will follow swiftly. All the elements required for recognition are present, and I recommend that we recognize the new regime promptly in order better to enable us to cultivate good relations with it and to influence it in the right direction.President Eisenhower noted his approval on the source text.

div.head: ES–29. Telegram from the Secretary of State to the Embassy in El SalvadorSource: Department of State, Central Files, 716.00/11–160. Secret; Niact. Drafted and signed by Mann.
div.p:
169. Principal lines our reasoning on recognition issue have been: 1.
Overthrow of Lemus regime was an accomplished fact. 2.
Our principal objective should be to support promptly those elements who are willing and able to prevent a Castro-Communist take-over and to guide evolution towards a constitutional regime oriented toward West. 3.
Osorio appeared to be best, if not only person around whom Army and anti-communist elements could unite to bring about such transition. Corollary to this is our belief that division and drift at this time in El Salvador would create a climate propitious for commie take-over.

Embtels 244 and 248In telegram 244 from San Salvador, November 1, 1960, the Chargé, Downs, reported Colonel Osorio apparently did not intend to attempt to prevent any party from participating in any election or to curb Communist propaganda and organizational activities. (716.00/11–160) In telegram 248 from San Salvador, November 1, 1960, Downs informed the Department of State of a Communist-line, anti-U.S. radio broadcast in San Salvador on October 31, and reported that the government controlled station was dropping the USIS daily prepared international newscast. (716.00/11–160) are disturbing because they suggest Osorio may be unwilling to prevent intensive propagation of communist propaganda in El Salvador and that he has no plans to prevent communist and Castroites from promptly organizing as a political force.

If you concur we suggest Downs approach Osorio promptly
and inform him that while Department has no desire to intervene in Salvadoran political crisis we believe we have common interest in preventing Communist-Castro take-over. In view of esteem with which he is held in U.S. we would appreciate knowing whether he agrees that a failure to stand up to Communist and Castroites at this critical time will create serious danger of chaos and confusion which will afford maximum opportunity for Communists and their Castro allies to take over. You should also attempt discreetly to ascertain what his detailed views are on this subject. If possible ascertain how he intends meet this aspect of problem. You should also seek to ascertain what Osorio’s estimate is of his ability control Army and if you deem this prudent his plans for unifying Army. Depending on how conversation has gone up to this point and whether you agree with approach suggested in paragraph
next following, you may also wish inform Osorio of plan to approach key Army officers.

If in your opinion split among officer corps is serious, we suggest an approach should also be made promptly to key officers in both Osorio and Lemus camps. These officers would be informed that while we have no desire to intervene in political affairs of Salvador and in particular no desire to take sides as between military groups, we believe that unity of armed forces in face of present Communist threat is both urgent and essential. Colonel Alberto Escamilla or
Major Ruben Rosales or both may be best persons to approach in Osorio camp. General Molina or General Cordova or both might be best persons to approach in Lemus group. However, our information regarding military is fragmentary and we leave to Embassy’s and Mil Attaches discretion which officers should be approached and most appropriate person in Embassy family to make approach. Cable Niact results these conversations with any additional recommendations Embassy may have. Department suspending recognition until receipt your report.
Ambassador Kalijarvi concurs.

div.head: ES–30. Telegram from the Chargé in El Salvador (Downs) to the Department of StateSource: Department of State, Central Files, 716.00/11–360. Secret; Niact. This telegram was sent in two sections.
div.p: 258. Department pass Army for ACSI; CINCARIB; CG USARCARIB; Department of Air Force for AFCIN. Re Department telegram 169.See Document ES–29.

At “Kye” Quinonez’s house and in company Colonel Matthews spent one hour this morning with Osorio, and hour with junta member Major Rosales alone, two hours with Rosales and Colonel Escamilla together. Quinonez party to all discussions.

Made presentation as suggested reference telegram and Osorio commenced with review of situation leading to coup which general in nature and lacking in specifics. Lemus hated by everyone, army disunited and decaying, several coup plots in making, executive without
power to control situation and action imperative to save country from anarchy.

With one exception, his replies to direct questions were extremely vague and evasive. He denied most emphatically that single Communist appointed to position in government. Some were anti-American but this did not make them Communists. He does not agree that failure to stand up to Communists at this time presents a danger. He does not see a need to curb Communist activities, organizationally or propaganda-wise, and all parties will be given opportunity to participate in free elections. Said he erred in exiling Communists when he was President. Should have kept them here and channeled their activities. No more than 25 real Communists in country at
present time and plan now is to “canalizar” their activities; they would be watched and made use of. He implied without saying so directly that if need be proper action could be taken at proper time. Questioned he said he thought he had sufficient influence on junta to initiate control measures at proper time if needed. Specific instances of present open Communist activities such as the inflammatory program of Radio Universal were pointed out to Osorio and his only comment was “this is natural.” When asked explicitly whether or not he anticipated that a 6-man junta could efficiently function or even last with inefficient operation for a period of two years until forthcoming elections, he circumvented the question and gave an explanation of how the military members of the junta had been permitted to select 50 percent of the new government assignments and how the civilian members of the junta had selected the remaining 50 percent. What needed now was unity so that urgently needed social and economic programs can be implemented. Changes had to occur within three months or serious threat to government will emerge from people. Support of extreme left as well as right needed for this and any restrictive action against former would disrupt unity and therefore could not be entertained. He not taking a direct part in affairs of junta but providing his counsel and advice. He reiterated throughout that army united and in control of situation but remarked on several different occasions that situation very delicate. Osorio readily agreed to suggestion we talk with selected army officers and suggested Major Rosales and Colonel Escamilla.

Osorio said government would abide by international agreement[s]. Asked about economic integration treaties said these could go on but some of things agreed to would have to be changed. Could not for example permit free flow of corn into this country. U.S. could produce it too cheaply and too many Salvadorans depended on it for a livelihood. Present situation this regard chaotic. Did
not know enough about proposal for new Central American bank to comment. Would have to be studied.

We found Major Rosales straightforward, honest, pro-Western and friendly but a complete babe in the woods. He admitted military on junta consulting with Osorio and that civilian side probably not under Osorio’s direction. Clear he has serious doubts about Doctor Fabio Castillo; he asked whether we could confirm he had extreme leftist leanings. Said decision junta taken by majority vote and no one leader. Admitted that if disagreements occurred and could not be resolved through discussion, they put aside for later. Saw dangers in this arrangement but for moment junta working well together.

Questioning brought out he totally ignorant re developments outside junta. When filled in he clearly taken aback and started taking notes. Said he did not know many of those appointed government positions, clarifying that Salazar Rodezno nominated for Information Chief Casa Presidential by junta member Falla Caceres. Asked whether intention existed apply any curbs Communist activities he parroted Osorio’s remark re strategy permitting open, unfettered operations until Communists identified. When asked who first presented the strategy he hesitated and then answered: “Rene Fortin Magana”. When pressed as to plans for controlling Communist movement Rosales reaffirmed that no plan existed. Said he was very inexperienced in this new assignment and would welcome any suggestions we might have to solve problem without being accused of curbing civil liberties. He stated that military members of junta felt that economic measures improve lot lower classes must be initiated immediately but that civilian members were standing firm in their position that political orientation of government must take precedence. He concluded that military members junta charged with security while civilian members dealing with political situation.

Colonel Escamilla arrived and Rosales gave him straight forward account our talk to that point, including our concern re Communist infiltration and activities. Escamilla inclined at first brush these off saying most effective way
handle these was through economic deeds rather than words or control measures. Turning to Quinonez he remarked that he and people he represented should immediately join government in these activities. Quinonez asked whether Escamilla aware type propaganda now being put out by Communists. I called for tape recording (Embassy telegram 248) and for first time Quinonez himself, Escamilla and Rosales heard what Communists saying. Reaction electric with much shaking of heads. All agreed this pure Communism rather than nationalism and that action some sort seemed called for, but they continued expound difficulties taking any direct action under existing circumstances. I suggested good place to start was with Salazar Rodezno. Rosales and Escamilla departed saying they would look into matter.

Quinonez who in interim between Osario’s departure and Rosales arrival had made effort defend some of Osorio’s remarks made no
further attempt to do so upon conclusion three interviews. Impact all that is happening seemed to dawn upon him for first time. Asked directly whether in face all he had heard he would, if in my position, recommend recognition this government, he replied he could not in all honesty give an answer. He was not enough of a politician or diplomat to be able to assess all pros and cons of extending or not extending recognition. One thing for certain, situation extremely critical and all help and advice U.S. could give was urgently needed.

[text not declassified] If this could be done without recognition, recognition now not overriding. On my way to Embassy intercepted by emissary from Roberto Parker, He told me Parker had asked him come to see me to transmit following message: Parker had visit yesterday from Major Castro Moran,
from Escuela de Guerra. Major Moran told Parker that the military was very unhappy over the current situation. He said that he was speaking for the majority and that they were thinking of doing something about it. Parker asked Moran why he had come to him. He replied that he had come because Parker could put him in touch with American Embassy. Parker replied he did not want to become involved, but that he did have a very good friend in the military, a Major Rodriguez Simo, in the Escuela Militar and that if this man would come and see him he would talk with him. Simo came to see Parker last night. He told him much the same thing that Moran had, adding that their group now had the support of every army unit with the exception of the national guard. Simo said, additionally that Colonel Yanes and Captain Rosales in the current junta were also unhappy and had expressed private regrets over the way the coup was handled and how it was turning out. The emissary said that Parker had also told him to pass on to me that when he had seen me two nights ago he had thought that the U.S. should not recognize. He said he had since talked to many responsible people plus these in the army and that all now agreed emphatically that U.S. should not recognize this junta. Parker said in addition he now sure good many people were not happy with Osorio. He was told by his military visitors that Osorio did not carry out some of the commitments that he had made with the military prior to the coup. He said he is convinced from his recent talks that when next coup comes, and which he now believes it will Osorio will not be included therein. Separate telegram with our analysis follows. Briefly put, we strongly of view that recognition should be deferred indefinitely.
This may be considered joint Embassy/ARMA telegram.

div.head: ES–31. Memorandum from the Assistant Secretary of State for Inter-American Affairs (Mann) to the Acting Secretary of StateSource: Department of State, S/S–NSC (Miscellaneous) Files, Lot 66 D 95, “NSC–5902-Memoranda.” Secret. Drafted by Gwynn and Higdon.

list.head: SUBJECT
list.item: Recent Developments in El Salvador.

list.head: REF
list.item: NSC paper dated October 30 entitled “Coup d’etat in El Salvador.”Reference presumably is to the paper from Mann to Herter, October 31, 1960, See Document ES–27.

div.p: In the past week it has become clear that currently the most prominent if not the dominant figure in the revolutionary movement which overthrew the Lemus Government is ex-President Oscar Osorio who, while a complex individual, has a long record of cooperation with the U.S. and of opposition to Communist domination of El Salvador’s political life. In this coup he appears to have had the financial support of some of the leading “14 families.” There is, however, a question as to whether he is in full control of the situation with indications that the influence of the extreme left may be growing rapidly and unchecked. Also, there are reports of dissension in the military and plans for a counter-coup by dissident officers. The question of the recognition of the new Salvadorian regime is being given urgent consideration in the light of these reports as this paper is being prepared.

The most significant new indications of expanding Castro-Communist influence include: a)
The appointment of more leftists to second and third echelon positions in the Government, particularly in the Attorney General’s office, the Ministries of Education and Labor, the Supreme court (two to three seats in nine seat body), and in the Junta public relations office. Among these are some extremists or Communists. b)
The commencement of a daily half-hour radio program carrying the straight Communist line, reportedly with the blessing of the new Junta public relations office, and the cancellation of a USIS daily prepared international newscast on the Government-controlled station (since reinstated). c)
The rapid resumption of activities by Communist-dominated groups, including the reappearance of manifestos making demands on the Government apparently designed to foment unrest and keep it moving toward the left; the resumption of public student meetings;
efforts to intimidate University students and faculty members opposing the Communist student leadership in the recent disturbances; and the arrest on a vague assault charge of an ex-deputy who had pushed hard for anti-Communist legislation before the fall of Lemus. d)
The reported return from exile of Cuban “Prensa Latina” staffers, rumored plans for the re-opening of the Cuban Embassy in El Salvador and rumors regarding plans for the creation of a civilian militia.

The new Government appears to lack agreement on any real doctrine and it certainly contains anti-U.S. elements, with the inherent risk that these, though in a minority at present, could possibly take over. Col. Osorio admits that the situation is delicate. He appears to be influencing the three military members of the six-man Junta, but possibly has less influence on the civilian members. While he has implied to our Charge that proper action would be taken when the time came, he apparently does not intend to curb Communist activities, organizationally or propaganda-wise, at present. He feels this kind of a coalition is necessary and desirable at this time.

On the question of recognition, Ambassador Kalijarvi, presently here on consultation, and the Embassy recommend deferring recognition indefinitely. They consider that the complexion and trend of the present Government is leftward towards a Castro-Communist takeover; that the reported plans for a counter-coup may make it short-lived; that recognition would cast a cloak of respectability about the new Government in the eyes of other countries and peoples and encourage attempts to effect similar overthrows elsewhere in Central America; and that immediate recognition would thus encourage and strengthen forces hostile to the United States without any realistic prospect of our being able to control the situation or to effect a change in the course of the new government.

There is, of course, always a possibility that Communist-Castro elements will succeed in getting an upper hand in El Salvador. The question is, however, whether it is in the U.S. interest to work with the new Government and endeavor, through the moderate elements of the regime, and particularly Osorio, to achieve an orientation toward the West, or whether, by failure to recognize or delay in recognition, we should alienate the Government, weaken Osorio and help to create a situation of uncertainty propitious for Communist and Castro influence. On balance, recognizing there are risks in whatever we do, I believe we can more effectively pursue U.S. objectives by working with the present Government. This conclusion is based largely on the hope that Osorio will remain influential, and the history of our relations with Osorio.

div.head: ES–32. Memorandum of Discussion at the 466th Meeting of the National Security CouncilSource: Eisenhower Library, Whitman File, NSC Records. Top Secret. Eyes Only. This memorandum was prepared by Robert H. Johnson, Director of the NSC Planning Board Secretariat, on November 8, 1960. The source text contains a list of 27 attendees.
div.p: [Here follows discussion of agenda items 1–4, concerning outer space programs, Cuba, significant world events affecting U.S. security (Sino-Soviet clash, Laos El Salvador), and Algeria. Portions printed below are from the merged discussion of items 3 and 4.]

Dealing next with El Salvador, General Cabell said that the Communists and pro-Castro forces were making a strong bid for power. Ex-President Osorio, who had used these forces as a means of getting back to power, had appointed pro-Communists and pro-Castro individuals to the Cabinet and other posts. Osorio thought he could control these elements but they have moved quickly to reinforce their position. They have appointed Communists and pro-Communists to second and third echelon positions in the government and were moving in on information and propaganda media. They are also demanding removal of all Osorio’s supporters. Osorio hopes to rule El Salvador indirectly until the 1952 elections. He says that he cannot consider plans to restrict the extreme Left because he needs their support to get action on certain reform measures. The army was apprehensive and a group of officers had plans for salvaging the dominant position of the military. They must act quickly, however, if their action is to be effective. General Cabell suggested that control of El Salvador by pro-Castro elements would pose a series threat to Guatemala.
[Here follows discussion of possible Soviet intervention in Algeria.]

Secretary Merchant went on to point out that the U.S. had not yet recognized the new government in El Salvador although we are considering the matter on a 24-hour basis. We had thought it unwise to recognize the government in view of the possibility of a counter-coup by conservative elements in the army. This was a difficult choice. The question was whether recognition would strengthen the reasonable elements in the government despite the fact that Leftist elements were honeycombing the government. Secretary Merchant expressed the view that Osorio may well have been double-crossed. He said that a decision would be needed within the next 24–72 hours. If we waited too long and there was no counter-coup, we would lose our ability to influence those who are our friends in the existing government.

The President observed that it was frightening how a few Communist elements could get in and take over a government while the others in the government behaved like jellyfish. It was also alarming that we could not get the OAS to be really concerned about such a situation because of the political problems that these governments have at home. He observed that we might have to go back to greater reliance on power politics.

Mr. Mann stated that a decision on recognition had to be made on the basis of an estimate of whether the existing El Salvador Government would be around long enough to make support worthwhile or whether we should work for a counter-revolution. The President suggested that we ought to find out whether the Rightists in El Salvador believe that it would be useful for us to recognize the regime or whether they consider that withholding recognition would be helpful in stimulating a counter-coup. Secretary Merchant observed that U.S. recognition could dishearten the opposition. The President asked whether we were talking to the opposition. Mr. Mann said that we were and that a majority of our friends in the governments were urging prompt recognition. However, he also acknowledged that friendly army officers took the opposite view. Secretary
Anderson said that he did not see how could run a government with the second and third echelons in the control of the Communists and the top of the government split; he did not see how any government could long exist on this basis on our side. Secretary Gates expressed the view that we should drag our feet on recognition because recognition would create a UN problem; that is, it would provide a basis for possible later UN intervention. He felt we were entitled to a period of time for foot dragging. The President stated that we did not want to let the situation sit and simmer; we needed to decide the best way to achieve our objectives. Secretary Merchant concluded this portion of the discussion by observing that there was no doubt that Osorio was friendly to us; the only question was whether he could control the situation.
The National Security Council:

3. Noted and discussed an oral briefing by the Acting Director of Central Intelligence on the subject, with specific reference to Sino-Soviet relations; the situation with respect to Algeria; and the situations in Laos and El Salvador.This paragraph constitutes NSC Action 2330, approved by the President on November 10, 1960. (S/S–NSC (Miscellaneous) Files, Lot 66 D 95, NSC Records of Action)
[Here follow the NSC Action on Algeria and discussion and Action on agenda item 5, Scandinavia.]

div.head: ES–33. Memorandum from the Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs (Merchant) to the Secretary of StateSource: Department of State, Central Files, 716.02/11–860. Secret. The source text bears the notation: “Overtaken By Events. 11/10/60.”

list.head: SUBJECT
list.item: El Salvador

div.p: Attached as Tab A is telegram to our Chargé a.i. in San Salvador approved by Tom Mann instructing him to inform the Foreign Minister immediately that the United States has decided to recognize the new government.Not filed with source text. The telegram was evidently not sent.
Although drafted for my signature, Mr. Mann feels that this should be approved before dispatch by you and the President.

Attached as Tab B is a memorandum from Ambassador Kalijarvi opposing this course of action.Not filed with the source text. The reference is presumably to Kalijarvi’s memorandum of November 6, 1960, which concluded with the statement that “immediate recognition of the junta government in El Salvador would encourage and strengthen forces hostile to the United States without any . . . prospect of our being able to control the situation in El Salvador and to effect the course of its government.” (ARA/OAP Files, Lot 63 D 127, “El Salvador, 1960”)

At the NSC meeting yesterday morning raised this subject with the President and outlined the pros and cons of recognition with an indication that the Department expected to have a recommendation for his consideration within a day or two. Although the discussion was brief, the main points were covered. Tom Gates expressed himself forcefully as opposed to recognition at this time. The others were silent, and the President gave no visible indication of judgment in the matter.

It is unnecessary to say that this is a very difficult decision with the factors pro and con closed balanced. I have in my own mind reached the conclusion that we should continue to delay according the junta recognition. The controlling reasons for this are: (1)
Having delayed this long, it is difficult to represent that recognition now would be automatic and containing no element of moral judgment. The passage of time itself will be construed as our having weighed all the factors and finally having come down on the side of recognition. (2)
Recognition now with a counter-coup still in the air would inevitably be a discouragement to those contemplating such
action. Certainly a counter-coup by moderate and anti-Communist army officers would be in our interest. (3)
On balance, I am dubious of our ability to exert effective influence in support of the moderates in the present junta, particularly with no Ambassador on the spot. Moreover, it seems to me the withholding of recognition, at least until the situation clarifies, in fact places some leverage in the hands of friends in the junta since they can hold out the prospect of recognition as an argument against further radical acts by the radical elements.
To recapitulate, I recommend withholding recognition and continuing to watch and wait.
I also recommend that you meet with Mr. Dillon, Mr. Mann, and myself as soon as convenient after your return for a further review of this matter.

div.head: ES–34. Memorandum for the President by the Secretary of StateSource: Eisenhower Library, Whitman File, International File. Secret. A notation by Brigadier General Goodpaster on the source text reads as follows: “President approved orally. I notified State Dept.”

item.hi: Recognition of Junta in El Salvador

div.p: As you know, we have delayed recognition of the Junta in El Salvador pending further analysis of its stability, composition and political orientation. It is now clear that the new Government is one of coalition without adequate leadership which, while seeking reform, has no clear idea of how to deal effectively with subversive elements. This presents a situation of danger and it may well be that we should recognize so as to be in the best position to use our influence to strengthen the efforts of non-Communists to orient government policy along democratic lines.

I recommend that you authorize me to extend recognition to the Junta Government at such time as we consider our interests will best be served by so doing. We are informed that Brazil has decided to recognize the Junta Government today. Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Panama, Ecuador, Paraguay, Israel, China, Austria and Spain have already recognized. I anticipate that other countries will soon follow suit.

div.head: ES–35. Letter from the Chargé in El Salvador (Downs) to the Ambassador in El Salvador, Temporarily in Washington (Kalijarvi)Source: Department of State, ARA/OAP Files, Lot 64 D 16, “Junta Memoranda: El Salvador, 1960.” Confidential. Kalijarvi enclosed this letter with a memorandum to Herter, November 16, 1960, opposing immediate recognition of the Junta and recommending his prompt return to El Salvador. (ARA/OAP Files, Lot 63D 127, “El Salvador, 1960”)
div.p: I received your two lettersThe letters under reference were not further identified. and wish to thank you very much for them and for the advice and counsel which I can read between the lines. We have been exceedingly busy. What with the many discussions we have been having with almost everyone around the place these days, the telegrams that have had to be drafted and cleared and the other myriad of activities which always seem to come upon one, I must admit that I have had very little time for either eating or sleeping. It has, however, as you can probably gather from that end, been a very interesting period. I believe that the pieces of the puzzle are beginning to fall into place fairly rapidly these days and I must say that the picture which is outlined is much as we had thought it would be in the early stages. One thing seems clear: we are in for a very difficult period over the next couple of months. From all we have been able to learn to date I am now more convinced than ever that we will be making a very grave error to put our money on Mr. Osorio. The latest we have heard is that he is drinking very heavily and is now letting it be known among his very close friends that he has indeed been double-crossed. It seems to me, therefore, that our best course of action for the present is to give every bit of under the table assistance we can to the moderate forces in the country—both outside the government and where we can find them inside—and attempt to awaken them to the danger which is clearly apparent and give all the help we can in organizing the fight against it. This I think can be done without recognition on our part and I continue to believe that we would be making a very grave error in recognizing this Junta as it is currently composed.

I think you too would be amazed at the number of people who have been seeking us out in the last week to tell us of their fears and concerns. People who up to a week ago were insisting that we recognize and
give this government our full assistance. Among them, I am sure, are a large number who contributed both financially and morally
to the overthrow of the Lemus regime. I think that they are now coming to realize that they have a bear by the tail—genesis Russian—and are now very much concerned about how to get rid of it. That it will be gotten rid of, at least in the form of the present Junta, I am convinced. Just how soon the very careful preparations that will be necessary for success will be ready is anyone’s guess. I don’t believe, however, that we will find the present situation existing at the end of this month. I hope we will be able to convince our peers in Washington to hold off for at least this long.
. . ..Four dots appear in the source text.
Most sincerely,

div.head: ES–36. Memorandum of Telephone Conversation, by the Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs (Merchant)Source: Department of State, Central Files, 716.02/11–1160.
div.p: Mr. Gray said Mr. Gates was terribly concerned about recognition of the new government of El Salvador. He was not in agreement with State. He was strongly opposed to going ahead as were the Joint Chiefs. He acknowledges that this was political and he understood that Allen Dulles was also opposed. Mr. Gray said he could not speak for Mr. Dulles but he thought this was correct information. He told Mr. Gates that he had not been in on the matter except for what came up in the National Security Council.Reference is to the NSC meeting of November 7; for the memorandum of discussion, see Document ES–32. He did not consider this to be an NSC matter and therefore had not inserted himself in the process, and he didn’t intend to except to pass along his point of view which is the same as Mr. Gates’. But this is an individual point of view because he would think the President would look to the Secretary of State for primary advice. However, [illegible in the original] would like to know how State felt it should be done—i.e., how do the people at the top feel—and more specifically how did Mr. Merchant feel about it.

Mr. Merchant said he would start with last [illegible in the original] about last night. Mr. Merchant had [illegible in the original] Gates through [illegible in the original] requesting that [illegible in the original] El Salvador until [text not declassified] was [illegible in the original]In notes on a telephone conversation of November 10, 1960, Merchant stated that Robert H. Knight, Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for International Security Affairs, called him on behalf of Secretary of Defense Gates, asking for delay of recognition pending receipt of information on the following day which might bear on the decision (716.02/11-1060) [illegible in the original] to arrive in [illegible in the original] Friday. Mr. Merchant [illegible in the original] so the situation has been held up. Although the Secretary has the President’s approval or discretionary [illegible in the original] recognize ES when it is timely and right. State’s [illegible in the original] yesterday was to recognize the country in a [illegible in the original] to watch developments. This decision was [illegible in the original] on the basis of findings of private emissaries [illegible in the original] advice from some of our top Latin American friends [illegible in the original] on balance that a counter-coup by the conservative elements in the army, contrary to our original hope was not [illegible in the original] for some months. One argument against recognition was that it would discourage any such movements by friendly [illegible in the original] There was also the question of how [illegible in the original] could best encourage and invigorate the friendly moderate element who are still in the junta before they are gobbled up by the dangerous elements. It is a delicate judgment.
Mr. Gray said that Defense and others against it are entitled to make their strong views known, but he still felt it is the primary action of the State Department.

A further development, Mr. Merchant continued [illegible in the original]
of just a few minutes ago. The USIB met this morning, and it is the unanimous view of the intelligence community that this is predominately a very bad crowd. That is no news to State. The Secretary and he are getting a memo from Hugh Cumming,See Document ES–37. who attended the meeting; and that judgment, which was concurred in by Allen Dulles, would be taken into consideration by Mr. Herter and himself. It will come down to a close and difficult question of psychological and political consideration.
Mr. Gray thanked him for the background information.

div.head: ES–37. Memorandum from the Director of Intelligence and Research (Cumming) to the Secretary of StateSource: Department of State, Central Files, 716.00/11–1160. Secret.

list.head: SUBJECT
list.item: Considerations of Intelligence Community Regarding Recognition of El Salvador.

div.p: I have been informed that a decision has been made to extend recognition to the government which has been formed in El Salvador following the overthrow of President Lemus on October 26. While this decision is beyond my scope, I do feel very strongly that it is our duty to put forth our considered judgment of the results that may flow from such recognition.

Since there is no time for a National Intelligence Estimate in this case, Mr. Dulles, The Director of Central Intelligence, suggests that we incorporate in one paper the view of representatives of the intelligence components of the Department of State, the Central Intelligence Agency, the Department of Defense, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and the Departments of the Army, Navy, and Air Force.

The government formed in El Salvador following the overthrow of President Lemus on October 26 continues to exhibit an increasing trend toward the left. A growing proportion of the Junta appointments to the cabinet and other important government posts are going to confirmed or suspected Communists. The individual responsible for engineering the coup was former President Osorio who had enlisted the support of military and wealthy civilian elements in addition to many leftists. It now appears that Osorio is unable, or perhaps unwilling to contain the growing power of the leftists who are becoming entrenched in the new regime. Although there are Junta and Cabinet members who show signs of concern over the situation, they have not demonstrated the capability of coping with their more politically skilled leftist colleagues. A counter-coup by disgruntled but disunited military elements remains a possibility. The leftist trend of the Junta in El Salvador has been indicated more by the nature of government appointments than by actions or declarations. Also a considered danger is that several more important Communist and leftist appointments and removals of moderate elements are pending the receipt of recognition by the United States Government.

Although the Junta has lifted the state of siege, the dissolution of Congress and the elimination of pro-Lemus elements, friendly to the
United States, and the vague promise of holding free elections two years hence, does not give an assuring picture of what future course of action the Junta will take.

United States Government recognition at this time would discourage the hopes of non-Communist opposition to carry out a counter-coup against the Junta. Recognition would provide the Junta with the respectability they now desperately are searching for. This would allow the leftists the needed time to consolidate their gains and to seek outside support from other leftist oriented governments, such as Cuba. After they become well entrenched, El Salvador would probably serve as a base for similar movements in neighboring countries. This perhaps is the major risk involved to the political stability and future security of Central America. A leftist dominated El Salvador could serve as a vital wedge, resulting in an extension of Castro-type Communism from Cuba to the Central American mainland. Castroism would then be provided with a West Coast opening—a base for seaborne Communist access to Central America. The current unrest and instability of Guatemala and Honduras are such that even the presence of a leftist government in El Salvador would provide the necessary spark needed to topple these shaky governments. Nicaragua also would not long be able to resist the presence of leftist governments in three neighboring Central American countries. The effects of such developments on Panama and the security of the Canal Zone are self-evident. A further problem would be posed to the U.S. Government in giving additional support to bolster countries thus threatened. As a final consideration, recognition of the present government of El Salvador by the U.S. would be widely interpreted throughout Latin America as well as inside the country, as approval of what could quite easily result in another Castro type regime.

The foregoing has been jointly drafted by senior representatives of the intelligence community and the conclusions approved by all of them, including The Director of Central Intelligence. In a memorandum to Herter, November 13, 1960, Mann took issue with Cumming’s memorandum and strongly urged that the United States “proceed forthwith to recognize the Junta Government.” (ARA/OAP Files, Lot 63 D 127, “El Salvador, 1960”)

div.head: ES–38. Telegram From the Embassy in El Salvador to the Department of StateSource: Department of State, 3 pages not declassified.
ES–39. Telegram from the Chargé in El Salvador (Downs) to the Department of StateSource: Department of State, Central Files, 716.00/11–236. Confidential; Niact; Limit Distribution.
div.p: 326. For Mann. Following from Stewart:C. Allan Stewart, Counselor of Embassy in Venezuela, visited San Salvador, November 20–23. A memorandum from Stewart to Mann, December 2 reporting on this visit, was enclosed with a letter from Stewart to Higdon, December 2 1960. (ARA/OAP Files, Lot 64 D 16, “Junta Correspondence: El Salvador, 1960.”)

After two hour meeting with Osorio, two hour session attended by all six members of Junta and about 15 interviews Salvadorans, Americans and others these are my observations: 1)
Osorio was key figure in overthrow. He and civilian elements were in accord sometime before overthrow. 2)
Osorio admits there will probably be counter attempts in armed forces and plotting is in evidence but based on my information Osorio has enough support in armed forces to keep present Government in power. Osorio has receded into background and provides occasional advice but three military members of Junta are his men and Minister InteriorCol. Alberto Escamilla. is strong type loyal to Osorio. Therefore, Osorio is key man in country. 3)
Civilian members of Junta are well-intentioned but inexperienced. I feel they are anxious to cooperate with U.S. If there were any doubt, however, Junta setup provides excellent check and balance with military members, backed by Osorio, exerting deciding influence. My meeting with Junta members was marked by frank exchange of ideas, especially on appointment people of doubtful ideology to Government
posts. They are aware of background these people and reached unanimous decision appoint them after
long debate. After conversing many serious Salvadorans I conclude there are sharply diverging opinions about whether doubtful individuals are Communists. In any event, Junta is aware our concern for some appointees and Osorio welcomed memorandum [text not declassified]The paper entitled, “Cuban Subersive Activities in E1 Salvador,” was not found in Department of State files. When translated “Osorio suggested it be given to Minister Interior Escamilla. 4)
Osorio and Junta are for free elections. They think Democratic forces can overwhelm Leftists at polls, and Osorio starts organizing new party to attract bulk of PRUD on Friday, with big convention around December 15. Civilian Junta members told me they discussed two types overthrow in first stages of plotting, namely à la Castro or à la Betancourt. Decided on latter because by Democratic forces in Venezuela won out later in free elections. Said this formula also had been successful in Guatemala and Honduras. Osorio said PRAM and CGTS will be controlled. Close friend one of military members Junta and of Minister Interior said these two strongly confirmed this fact to him. However, same source, evidencing his own concern, added that he had asked his friends if they sure they not being used. 5)
Junta admits its functions as caretaker Government while Congressional elections prepared is not enough and must make start on social program. Osorio said he had ideas along this line. 6)
Reaction among Salvadorans with whom I talked is regret for departure constitutional process but strong to mild feeling Lemus bungled student disturbances so badly his removal was logical aftermath. Return to constitutional Government is avowed unanimous desire. 7)
Consensus opinion is that any succeeding Government would be rightist military Junta. Some observers viewed this with alarm, saying it would not be accepted by liberal elements and masses, with consequent trouble.
8)
I am most impressed with attitude of intelligent Salvadorans who realize dangers of present situation and wish cooperate with Junta in finding solution along peaceful lines. Meanwhile working class continues at tasks without interruption. Cumbersome six-man Junta may be streamlined but I believe only after satisfactory agreement between civilians and military. 9)
Osorio made plea for recognition and Junta members were most eager get over point they wish to work with U.S. and need our support.

div.head: ES–40. Memorandum for the President by the Secretary of StateSource: Eisenhower Library, Whitman File, Dulles-Herter Series. Secret. Drafted by Coerr and Higdon. A memorandum from Herter to Goodpaster, November 25, 1960, suggested that he not put this matter before the President until Monday afternoon, November 28, to give the Department of Defense “an opportunity to register their dissent should they feel as strongly as they did in the past.” (Eisenhower Library, Whitman File, Dulles-Herter Series)

list.head: SUBJECT
list.item: Recognition of Junta in El Salvador

div.p: On November 11[10?], 1960 you authorized me to recognize the Junta Government of El Salvador at any time when I considered our interests would best be served by so doing. In view of doubts voiced by our intelligence community and others regarding the possible consequences of recognition, we sent a ranking Foreign Service Officer, who had until recently served as Director of the Office of Central American and Panamanian Affairs, to El Salvador to make an impartial survey of the problem. On the basis of numerous talks he held with persons in El Salvador, including American and Salvadorans with whom he had long been acquainted, the six-man Junta and former President Osorio, he has reported that Osorio seems to be the key figure behind the present Government and that the latter is attempting to maintain its independence of Castroist or Communist policies and personnel.See telegram 326 from San Salvador, November 30, 1960, Document ES–39. Mr. Allen Dulles and the Department of State’s Director of IntelligenceHugh S. Cumming, Jr. on the basis of this officer’s report and their judgment of current developments in El Salvador, no longer have any objection to recognition. I therefore propose to extend recognition on or about November 30, 1960 unless you perceive objection.According to a notation on the source text, President Eisenhower approved the memorandum on recognition, December 1, 1960.

div.head: ES–41. Letter from the Secretary of Defense (Gates) to the Secretary of StateSource: Department of State, Central Files, 716.02/11–2060. Secret.
div.p: Attached is the latest information available in Defense about the situation in El Salvador.The attachments were a paper and a memorandum. The paper, entitled “The Leftist Trend of the Government of El Salvador,” claimed that Communist influence had risen in the Salvadoran Government, student organizations, and labor movement, and it concluded that any action which strengthened the Junta would contribute to the rise of Communist influence on the future course of the Government. The second attachment, a memorandum of a telephone conversation between General Fitch and Lt. Col. Luther F. Long, General Staff, Chief, Western Hemisphere Section, Office of the Assistant Chief of Staff for Intelligence, on November 30, 1960, concerned efforts by the Communist-controlled CGTS to organize campesino committees throughout El Salvador The Defense intelligence holdings indicate a considerable Left activity by the Junta government, with confirmation of facts which have caused our previous concern. The confirmation includes information just received from General Alva FitchMaj. Gen. Alva R. Fitch, Deputy Assistant Chief Staff for Intelligence, Department of the Army, visited El Salvador, November 29-December 1, 1960. General Fitch met with numerous persons he had known during his assignment as military attaché in El Salvador 1948–1950. who is in San Salvador now and who is well acquainted with Central American affairs.
I wanted to be certain that this information was available to you.

Since the question of recognition primarily is one of political judgment, I will leave this up to you. However, we are so concerned at the prospects of Communist take-over, whether or not recognition is afforded the Junta, that I suggest the State Department, the Defense Department and CIA get together to determine what feasible actions can be taken to insure against the take-over.
Sincerely yours,

div.head: ES–42. Memorandum of Conversation with the President, Prepared by the President’s Staff Secretary (Goodpaster)Source: Eisenhower Library, Whitman File, “DE Diaries.” Secret. This memorandum was prepared on December 7, 1960.

list.head: OTHERS PRESENT
list.item: Secretaries Dillon and Irwin
General Goodpaster

div.p: Mr. Dillon and Mr. Irwin met briefly with the President to discuss a difference of view regarding recognition of the government which took power in El Salvador as a result of the recent coup. Mr. Dillon said he realized that Defense had receded from its position of offering objection, although he understood Defense still disagreed with the action. He said that the State Department view is that if the United States does not recognize the new government, we will be “throwing in the towel” so far as sending good people into the area to try to influence the situation. He said that State considers that if we extend this recognition, we will be able to hold off the Communist effort there.

He added that other Latin American countries have recognized the new regime, including Argentina, Brazil and Chile. He said that before extending recognition, we will ask the Salvadorans to make a statement whether they support OAS commitments. If so, we will recognize them. He added that the CIA supports this action, but that Defense takes the stand that the government there is more Communist-influenced than State believes is true.

Mr. Irwin said that Defense has thought that there might be a counter coup in the area. However, it has not developed. Defense has considered that we should avoid tying our hands in El Salvador as in Laos through hasty recognition of a regime which will come under Communist domination. He added that
Defense is concerned that recognition of Communist-oriented governments hurts our friends in other countries. However, Defense considers that the points have been brought out and they withdraw on the matter on the grounds that the question is one of State Department responsibility.
The President gave his assent to going ahead with recognition on the basis described by Mr. Dillon.
[Here follow discussion on Yugoslavia.]

div.head: ES–43. Telegram from the Acting Secretary of State to the Embassy in El SalvadorSource: Department of State, Central Files, 716.00/10–2760. Official Use Only; Priority. Drafted by Whitman and Higdon, and signed by Mann.
div.p: 232. Embtel 222.The referenced telegram, dated October 27, 1960, transmitted note No. 5039 from Déneke to Kalijarvi, October 27, described in the present telegram. (716.02/10–2760) The Ambassador is instructed in person to deliver to FONOFF on or about December 3 following note of recognition on part of United States of new Government of El Salvador:

“I have the honor to acknowledge the receipt of Your Excellency’s Note No. D-5039, dated October 27, in which you requested me to inform my Government that a Junta of Government has now been established in El Salvador. Your Excellency’s note states that the new Government has declared its intention to continue to comply strictly with the Constitution of 1950, which remains in force, to observe international treaties and conventions, to fulfill its obligations and commitments, and to respect human rights.

In view of the assurances set forth in your note and of the official affirmations made public concerning the holding of free elections, my Government has instructed me to state that it welcomes these assurances, and that it is pleased to extend recognition to the Junta of Government as the provisional Government of El Salvador.”

Please inform Department promptly of any changes in Note for accuracy and of time and manner delivery.Telegram 356 from San Salvador, December 3, 1960, informed the Department that Kalijarvi delivered the above note to Déneke, 6 p.m., December 3. (716.02/12–360)

div.head:
ES–44. Message from the Assistant Secretary of State for Inter-American Affairs (Mann) to Colonel Oscar OsorioSource: Department of State, Central Files, 716.02/12–260. In a memorandum to Mann dated November 30, attached to the source text, Merchant stated that “if the President approves prompt recognition of the junta in El Salvador, I feel strongly that whoever communicates to the junta our decision should see Osorio and tell him that . . . we have done so on certain assumption, i.e., that elections will be held within x months, that necessary steps will be taken to prevent the government falling under the control of Communists or Castro elements, and that the junta is interested in preserving traditionally friendly relations with the United States Government.” Mann’s letter did not convey the essence of Merchant’s request, but Osorio had already given the requisite assurances to Allan Stewart in San Salvador on November 21, according to Stewart’s memorandum to Mann, dated December 2, reporting on his visit to San Salvador; see footnote 1. A partially legible notation on Merchant’s memorandum possibly refers to that meeting.
The source text for Mann’s letter is an unsigned carbon copy. No record of its delivery was found in Department of State files.
div.p: I believe you will be pleased to know that the United States will soon recognize the provisional Junta Government of El Salvador.See telegram 232, Document ES–43.

I wanted to express my appreciation for the time which you so kindly gave to Allen Stewart and to let you know that our delay in recognition was not based on the belief that the highest officials of the Government are anti-democratic.
